title: Designing Cooperative Molecular Glues for FKBP12-MAPRE1 with Enhanced-Sampling Molecular Dynamics Simulations
paragraphs: Molecular glues (MGs) have emerged as a powerful modality in drug discovery, offering the unique ability to induce novel protein–protein interactions (PPIs) and target flat protein surfaces that have been previously considered inaccessible. − By stabilizing the interface between an E3 ligase (or another presenter protein) and a target protein, molecular glues can trigger downstream effects such as ubiquitination and degradation. , Compared to bifunctional PPI inducers such as proteolysis targeting chimeras (PROTACs), MGs often display higher cooperativity and are less susceptible to the hook effect (or prozone effect). − Cooperativity in induced-proximity systems has been described within the thermodynamic framework of three-body binding equilibria, while structural studies of PROTAC ternary complexes have demonstrated how favorable protein–protein interactions can drive cooperative ternary-complex formation. However, despite their potential, rational design and even optimization of molecular glues remain a significant challenge. While numerous computational approaches, including physics-based and machine learning methods, have been developed in recent years to facilitate ternary-complex prediction, these tools are still far from fully capturing the dynamics and determinants of cooperativity that govern ternary-complex formation (see the review in ref and references therein). Consequently, discovery often continues to rely on serendipity or extensive empirical screening. −

An example of this challenge is the system involving FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12) and MAPRE1 (microtubule associated protein RP/EB family member 1). In the recent work by Salcius et al., a macrocyclic MG R,S-SLF-1a ( 1a ) was discovered to induce interactions between FKBP12 and MAPRE1 ( Figure A). In the same work, the structure–activity relationship of the MAPRE1-recognition motif was studied by mutating two sites: the 4-piperidine moiety ( Figure A–B, circled in yellow) and the α-position ( Figure A–B, circled in red). Several modifications at the α-position of this site retain glue activity, but with a wide range of absolute cooperativity as determined by follow-up work ( Figure C and Table ). In contrast, modifications to the 4-piperidine moiety consistently impede MAPRE1 recruitment ( Figure D). The static picture from the crystal structure could not explain how these subtle changes influence cooperativity and glue activity.

In this work, we bridge the gap between the static structural data and observed cooperativity by investigating the dynamics of binary and ternary complexes using enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By extensively sampling the ensembles of the FKBP12-ligand complexes with and without MAPRE1 using replica exchange with solute scaling (REST2), we formulated the hypothesis that high cooperativity arises from the PPI in the specific “stabilized configurational space” that is shared in both ensembles. Based on the recently developed thermodynamic foundations of cooperativity, we established a computational pipeline to predict the cooperativity of new MG candidates. First, we proposed a model that correlates the experimental cooperativity and the computed PPI matrices by developing and evaluating the model using the previously reported variants of 1a . Subsequently, we applied the model to prospectively design novel variants of 1a and predict their cooperativity in silico . Five candidates were synthesized and experimentally tested (together with resynthesis and retesting of five previous compounds). Three of the novel compounds exhibit an apparent cooperativity similar to or higher than the previously known most cooperative retested compound 11 . Another one shows an apparent cooperativity similar to the second-most cooperative retested compound 6 . Our results demonstrate that incorporation of conformational dynamics and induced PPI analysis is a viable strategy for the rational design and optimization of cooperative MGs.

To investigate the difference between the inactive compounds and the active ones, four active compounds covering a wide range of apparent cooperativity ( 1a , 8 , 10 , and 11 , see Figure C) and four inactive compounds ( 1d , 2a , 2c , and 2d , see Figure D) were studied in the ternary complex (FKBP12-ligand-MAPRE1 = FLM) with MD simulations for 1 μs (three replicates). In addition, a ligand-free (apo) system was also simulated for comparison. During the simulations, a dynamic interface between the two proteins was observed, which sees the fluctuating formation and disappearance of “native” and “nonnative” contacts between FKBP12 and MAPRE1, differing mainly by the tilt motion of MAPRE1 ( Figure A–B). “Native” contacts are PPIs observed in the available crystal structure of the ternary complex, whereas PPIs only seen in the simulations are considered “nonnative”. While the apo system quickly lost most of the native contacts (as expected due to the very low affinity of FKBP12 to MAPRE1 in the absence of glues), no significant differences in terms of PPI contacts were observed between inactive and active compounds within the simulation time scale ( Figure C–D).

Next, we analyzed the pairwise interaction energies in the FLM ensembles with MM/GBSA. , Note that the interaction energies measured here only account for the interactions in the ternary ⟨⟩ FLM state and do not take into account the entropic effects before the ternary complexation. All eight compounds exhibit similar interaction energies with FKBP12, ⟨ Δ E F − L i n t ⟩ F L M ( Figure E), which agrees with the experimental findings that the modifications of 1a in the 4-piperidine moiety do not alter its affinity for FKBP12. , Similarly, the interaction energy between the protein partners, ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M , is largely unaffected by the type of ligand binding ( Figure F). On the other hand, the MAPRE1-ligand interaction energy, ⟨ Δ E M − L i n t ⟩ F L M , shows statistical significance between active and inactive compounds ( p = 1.881 × 10 –3 at the compound level and p = 2.126 × 10 –5 at the interface level, Figure G). This suggests that inactive compounds cannot induce the ternary complex due to the dual-binding criterion (i.e., a molecular stabilizer needs to possess some affinity for both proteins). Interestingly, while in most simulations of the active compounds more than 40% of the contacts between the two proteins were native (i.e., native contact ratio >0.4), the inactive compounds show an anticorrelation between the MAPRE1-ligand interaction strength and the native contact ratio (Spearman’s correlation coefficient ρ = −0.81 for inactive compounds, Figure H), which is consistent with the hypothesis that firm interaction between the ligand and MAPRE1 stabilizes ternary complex configurations that contain many native contacts. Further analysis of the time series of these features and the RMSD of each component is shown in Section S2 in the Supporting Information .

In contrast to other macrocyclic MGs such as cyclosporine A, FK506, and rapamycin, compound 1a in the FKBP12-MAPRE1 system shows a significant conformational discrepancy between the crystal structures of the binary and ternary complexes ( Figure A–B). Superposition of the crystal structures of FL (PDB ID: 9DCW) and FLM (PDB ID: 9CO5) shows that FKBP12 and the FKBP12-binding motif of 1a ( Figure A) remain rigid upon recruitment of MAPRE1 (TM score: 0.98). However, the MAPRE1-recognition motif of 1a adopts an alternative conformation in the ternary complex to avoid a steric clash with MAPRE1 ( Figure A). To characterize the conformational change of the MAPRE1-recognition motif between the binary and ternary complexes, we define the intermotif angle θ lig by computing the angle formed by the planes fitted on the two motifs ( Figure B). This angle θ lig corresponds to −35.06° in the FL structure and 32.63° in the FLM structure. The difference in the ligand configuration implies the necessity of a conformational selection and/or induced-fit mechanism during the FL to FLM formation process, which is not immediately clear from the static structures. A detailed description of the protocol to calculate θ lig is provided in Section S3 in the Supporting Information .

When monitoring θ lig in the conventional MD simulations of the binary (FL) and ternary (FLM) complexes, we noted differences between the three replicates, which suggested convergence issues ( Section S4 of the Supporting Information ). Thus, we performed enhanced-sampling MD simulations using REST2; only the REST2 results are shown in the following. In the FL and FLM simulations, θ lig peaked around the values observed in the crystal conformations ( Figure C–D). Notably, the simulations occasionally sampled a conformation with θ lig around zero in both FL and FLM ensembles ( Figure C–D), which we termed the intermediate ligand conformation. In the FLM complexes, this intermediate conformation coincides with the bending motion of MAPRE1, characterized by a large angle θ PPI between three helical domains shown in Figure C. As a similar intermediate ligand conformation is occasionally sampled in the FL ensemble, we hypothesize that these low-probability intermediate conformations in both ensembles could explain a MAPRE1 recruitment pathway, as discussed in the next section.

To determine whether the intermediate conformations can also be adopted by other active compounds, we studied seven active compounds reported in ref : 3 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , and 11 . In addition to the FL and FLM complexes, REST2 simulations were performed for the ligands alone in the aqueous solution. Figure E shows that all compounds can adopt a range of conformations with θ lig between ±80 ◦ when free in solution. When bound to FKBP12 (FL ensemble), only conformations with θ lig values between negative and around zero are accessible, which indicates that the binding pocket restricts the flexibility of the macrocycles. Intriguingly, conformations with negative θ lig values are no longer reachable when MAPRE1 binds to the FL binary complex to form the ternary complex. Instead, zero to positive θ lig are found for the ligands in the FLM ensemble. The fact that binding of MAPRE1 induces a stable ligand conformation that is rarely observed in the FL ensemble highlights the cooperative interplay between the ligand conformation, the ligand-MAPRE1 interaction, and native PPI contacts, which we shall discuss in the next section.

The observation of a distinct yet overlapping conformational space in Figure E suggests that the formation of the ternary complex may be facilitated by both conformational selection and the induced-fit mechanism. This means that there is a subregion of the configurational space (ensemble) of the binary FKBP12-ligand complex that is suited for recruitment of MAPRE1. Similarly, there is a subregion of the configurational space of the ternary complex where the conformations of FKBP12 and the ligand overlap with conformations observed in the binary complex. In the following, we call these subregions of the binary and ternary ensembles the stabilized configurational spaces , which we denote with the superscript s . The superscript * is used to denote the minimal-energy configuration revealed by crystallography. Based on our observations from the MD simulations, we can formulate a hypothesis for the binding pathway, which is depicted in Figure A.

(A): Hypothesis of the FKBP12-ligand-MAPRE1 recruitment process. MAPRE1 (M) is shown in orange, ligand (L) in gray, and FKBP12 (F) in blue. The star superscript in FL * and FLM * indicates the minimal-energy configuration in the ensemble and the s superscript denotes the stabilized configurational space. (B–C): Correlation between the experimentally observed cooperativity and the computed PPIs between FKBP12 and MAPRE1 using all configurations (B) or using only the stabilized configurational space in the ternary ensemble (C).

First, the ligand in the FL complex could transition from the low-energy configuration (i.e., θ lig ≤ −10°, FL *) to the stabilized configuration FL s (where −10° ≤ θ lig ≤ 10°). Second, MAPRE1 is recruited by weak ligand-MAPRE1 interactions and nonnative PPI contacts (this step can be viewed as conformational selection). Once the FLM complex is formed in the stabilized configurational space (FLM s , where −10° ≤ θ lig ≤ 10°), the ligand undergoes another conformational change in the third step to strongly bind MAPRE1 and to induce native PPI contacts (FLM*, where θ lig ≥ 10°). The common ligand conformation shared in the FL s and FLM s ensembles is highlighted in the inset box of Figure A. Note that the putative pathway presented here is derived from observations from the equilibrium simulations and does not exclude alternative pathways of ternary-complex formation.

According to the thermodynamics of cooperativity, the precise identification of such stabilized configurational space in the FLM ensemble provides us with an opportunity to compute (and subsequently predict, see below) the cooperativity of the system. If we do not consider this stabilized configurational space and naively compare the FKBP12-MAPRE1 interaction energy calculated over the full ensemble ( ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M ) with the experimentally observed cooperativity, the correlation is not very good (Spearman coefficient ρ = 0.45, Figure B). The correlation is significantly improved (ρ = 0.90, Figure C) when considering only frames of the stabilized configurational space to compute the interaction energy between the two proteins ( ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M s ) . To determine this stabilized configurational space in practice, we aligned the FKBP12 structures frame-to-frame to compute whether a configuration of FL observed in the ternary FLM ensemble has a nonzero probability to occur in the binary FL ensemble (see Figure S41 in Section S5 in the Supporting Information for a schematic depiction of the procedure). Section S5 also contains more details about the frame-to-frame alignment procedure. Note that as the model was developed using only eight previously reported compounds, the retrospective correlation should be interpreted as model development rather than independent validation. The prospective compounds were selected before experimental testing, and their experimental results were not used to refit the model.

Encouraged by the high correlation between the experimental cooperativity and ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M s , our objective was to look for derivatives of 1a that show similar or higher cooperativity. We noticed that the two most cooperative compounds 10 and 11 ( Table ) have two geminal substituents at the α-position in the MAPRE1-recognition motif (red circle in Figure A). Furthermore, the substituent(s) at the α-position of four of the five most cooperative compounds ( 11 , 10 , 3 , and 1a ) are lipophilic. Based on these considerations, we screened commercial catalogues for amino-acid building blocks with two geminal substituents where the D -substituent is a methyl group (or part of a ring) and the L -substituent is lipophilic. As compound 6 , which showed the third highest cooperativity of the full set has a hydroxymethyl substituent at the α-position, we also considered some polar L -substituents. This produced 17 candidates, from which 12 were retained for prospective simulations based on their size and compatibility with the molecular-glue scaffold ( p0-pB , Figure A). We used the same procedure as described in the previous section and the model fitted from the parent compounds to estimate their cooperativity ( Figure B). From this, compounds p0 , p2 , p3 , p4 , and p6 were predicted as the most cooperative compounds and were submitted for synthesis and experimental validation. As a control, the lead compound ( 1a ), a moderately cooperative compound ( 6 ), a weakly cooperative compound ( 9 ), the most cooperative compound ( 11 ), and an inactive compound ( 1d ) from the literature were also resynthesized and tested in the same assays.

Absolute cooperativity α can be determined experimentally by either measuring K F‑L and K F‑LM or by measuring K M‑L and K FL‑M ( Figure A). However, due to the limits of the experimental assay, no exact binary binding affinity between the ligands and MAPRE1, K M‑L , could be determined ( E C 50 b i n a r y M A P R E 1 > 500 μ M ) and thus no absolute cooperativity could be obtained. The MAPRE1-binding titration experiment is discussed in Section S6.2 in the Supporting Information . Instead, we calculate the apparent cooperativity as the ratio of the binary and ternary EC50 values ( α a p p F K B P 12 = E C 50 b i n a r y F K B P 12 / E C 50 t e r n a r y F K B P 12 ) by titrating the corresponding ligand to 40 nM labeled FKBP12 with or without the presence of 10 μM MAPRE1. For example, an apparent cooperativity α a p p F K B P 12 = 7 is observed for compound 1a , indicated by the shift in EC50 values in the presence of 10 μM MAPRE1 ( Figure B). The ranking of the α a p p F K B P 12 values of the known compounds agrees overall well with the absolute cooperativity α abs reported in ref ( Figure C). Figure D summarizes α a p p F K B P 12 for each compound computed from the FKBP12-binding assay. In line with previous findings that compound 1d , an epimer of 1a , binds strongly to FKBP12 but cannot recruit MAPRE1, we find weak or no cooperativity ( α a p p F K B P 12 < 1 ) for 1d in the new experiments. The active compounds 11 , 9 , and 6 exhibit apparent cooperativity ranging from 8 to 41. From the five prospective compounds, only p3 shows little cooperativity ( α a p p F K B P 12 = 2.2 ± 0.4 , Figure D). Three compounds yielded apparent cooperativity similar to or greater than that of the best parent compound 11 ( α app FKBP 12 = 41 ± 13 ) : p0 (38 ± 11), p2 (39 ± 9), and p6 (81 ± 44). Compound p4 (21 ± 7) showed apparent cooperativity similar to that of the second-best retested parent compound 6 (24 ± 7).

Besides the ligand cooperativity α, protein cooperativity γ can also be calculated ( Figure A). Since the dissociation constant between the two proteins K F − M D is independent of the compound, the relative value of the protein cooperativity is equivalent to the ratio of ternary dissociation constants γ 1 / γ 2 = K F L 2 − M D / K F L 1 − M D . The MAPRE1-reporter EC50 ratio is used as an assay-derived relative apparent-cooperativity metric under the same assay conditions and is not interpreted as absolute thermodynamic cooperativity. In Figure E, we show a good correlation (Pearson coefficient r = 0.77) between the apparent cooperativities α a p p F K B P 12 and γ a p p M A P R E 1 relative to the lead compound 1a measured by different labeled proteins, providing a strong cross-assay concordance.

In summary, we achieved our goal to rationally design novel variants with higher cooperativity based on the observations from the MD simulations. These positive results highlight the power of considering a dynamic picture in the design of molecular glues.

The rational design and optimization of molecular glues has long been hindered by the complexity of predicting the protein–protein interface dynamics. In this study, we demonstrated that the cooperativity of macrocyclic molecular glues for the FKBP12-MAPRE1 system cannot be adequately explained by static crystal structures alone. By employing MD simulations, we could formulate a putative pathway for the formation of the ternary complex and successfully designed variants of the lead compound 1a with similar or higher cooperativity.

Our MD simulations suggest that the modifications of the 4-piperidine moiety fail to form the ternary complex because of the less favorable MM/GBSA interaction energies, which is consistent with weaker MAPRE1 engagement. Using enhanced sampling, we further revealed an intermediate conformation of the ligand, which is sampled in both the binary FKBP12-ligand and the ternary FKBP12-ligand-MAPRE1 ensembles. The observed ensemble overlap is consistent with a putative pathway involving conformational selection followed by structural relaxation, although the equilibrium simulations do not establish the kinetic sequence. By only considering the configurations in the intermediate state, which we call the stabilized configurational space, a high correlation (Spearman coefficient ρ = 0.90) was found between the computed interaction energy between the two proteins in the ternary complex and the experimentally measured absolute cooperativity. Using this model, we estimated the cooperativity of a library of 12 prospective variants of lead 1a and selected five for synthesis and experimental testing. Of these five novel compounds, four showed higher apparent cooperativity than the parent lead compound 1a , and three of them showed similar or greater apparent cooperativity than the previously most cooperative compound 11 .

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to elaborate on the conformational changes of molecular glues upon the third-body binding event and to prospectively design highly cooperative glues by establishing and targeting the stabilized configurational space shared between binary and ternary ensembles using MD simulations. We anticipate that this work will encourage researchers in the field to include considerations of protein and ligand dynamics in the design of cooperative molecular glues.

The initial conformations of the active molecular glue compounds were generated using the ConstrainedEmbed function of RDKit version 2023.03 using as a template the conformation of 1a in the crystal structure of the binary complex with FKBP12 (PDB ID: 9DCW) and of the ternary complex (PDB ID: 9CO5) respectively. The generated conformers were exported as an SDF file and converted to mol2 files and energy-minimized with the MMFF94 force field using OpenBabel 3.1.0. Because of the change in stereochemistry, inactive compounds 1d , 2a , 2c , and 2d were generated by the Builder in PyMOL v2.5.5 and saved as a mol2 file for later parametrization.

The initial coordinates of the complexes are taken from the crystal structures with ligand 1a (PDB IDs: 9DCW and 9CO5) either retained ( 1a ), removed (apo system), or replaced (other compounds). The AMBER ff19SB force field was used for proteins, GAFF2 , for the ligands, OPC for water molecules, and Joung/Cheatham ion parameters for Na + and Cl – ions. Partial charges of the ligands were assigned with the AM1-BCC method implemented in the program antechamber .

The constructed complexes were solvated in a water box with a length of 1.2 nm from the complex edge in each dimension with 0.15 M NaCl using the program tleap from AmberTools22. All simulations were performed with AMBER 22.

Energy minimization was performed for a maximum of 5,000 cycles, comprising 2,500 steps of steepest descent followed by up to 2,500 steps of conjugate-gradient minimization. A positional restraint with a force constant of 418.4 kJ mol –1 nm –2 was applied to proteins and ligand atoms during minimization. Equilibration comprised two consecutive 125 ps NVT stages followed by two consecutive 125 ps NPT stages. A time step of 1 fs was used during equilibration. Positional-restraint force constants of 418.4, 209.2, 209.2, and 41.84 kJ mol –1 nm –2 were applied to protein and ligand atoms during the four successive equilibration stages. Following equilibration, three production replicas were initiated from the final restart file of the second NPT stage. Although the replicas shared the same initial coordinates and velocities, they were propagated using independently initialized Langevin random streams generated with the AMBER 22 default setting ig = −1 .

Simulations were carried out with a Langevin thermostat to keep the temperature at 295.15 K with a collision frequency of 1.0 ps –1 and a Monte Carlo barostat to keep the pressure at 1 bar. A nonbonded cutoff distance of 1 nm was used with PME , to treat the long-range electrostatic interaction. The simulations were integrated with a time step of 2 fs, using the SHAKE algorithm to constrain the bond lengths of bonds involving hydrogen with a relative geometrical tolerance of 10 –6 . The translational and rotational center-of-mass motion was removed every 1000 steps. Trajectories were printed every 500 ps in the production simulation for analysis.

For the enhanced-sampling simulations, the REST2 implementation in Amber22 called Replica Exchange with Arbitrary Degree of Freedom (REAF) was used by setting the flag gti_add_re = 6 . The scaling was only applied on the ligand degrees of freedom. A scaling factor (1-τ) between 1 and 0.4 was used with an even spacing in the linear scale between 12 replicas, i.e., τ k = {0.000, 0.05454, 0.10908, 0.16362, 0.21816, 0.27270, 0.32724, 0.38178, 0.43632, 0.49086, 0.54540, 0.59994}, where k indicates the replica index, was used for the binary and ternary complex simulations, and a linear scale between 14 replicas ranging between 1 and 0.25, i.e., τ k = {0.000, 0.05769, 0.11538, 0.17307, 0.23076, 0.28845, 0.34614, 0.40383, 0.46152, 0.51921, 0.57690, 0.63459, 0.69228, 0.74997}, was used for the ligand-only simulations. The enhanced-sampling simulations were initiated from the last frame of the second NPT equilibration and propagated for 200 ns with replica exchange attempted at every 100 steps. The exchange acceptance ratios were around 35% in the ligand-only and binary complexes, and around 20% in the ternary complexes between all neighboring replicas. The per-replica-pair exchange ratio is shown in Figure S37 in the Supporting Information . Trajectories of the REST2 simulations were printed every 20 ps. The analyses on the REST2 simulations were performed on the physical replica (τ 0 = 0).

From the crystal structure of the ternary complex with compound 1a , the “native” contacts between the two proteins were defined as the number of atoms from one protein within 5 Å of any heavy atom of the second protein using the nativecontact command from cpptraj in AmberTools22, which provides both native and nonnative contact counts. The same procedure was applied to the frames of the MD simulations. If an identified contact is not part of the “native” set obtained from the crystal structure, it was counted as “nonnative”. The native contact ratio was calculated as N nat /( N nat + N non‑nat ), where N nat and N non‑nat are the number of native and nonnative contact atoms. It indicates whether the interactions between the two proteins are similar to the ones observed in the ternary crystal structure.

As a simplified descriptor of the bending motion of the MAPRE1-binding core of the ligand observed between the binary and ternary crystal structures, the angle between the MAPRE1-binding core and the FKBP12-binding core ( Figure A) was calculated by measuring the angle between the two fitting planes, termed the intercore angle θ lig . A detailed description and illustration of the plane-fitting procedure is provided in Section S3 in the Supporting Information .

Active and inactive compounds were compared at both the compound and interface levels. For the primary compound-level analysis, the six interface values obtained from three simulations with two interfaces each were averaged for each compound, producing four compound-level observations per activity group. For the exploratory interface-level analysis, the six interface values from each compound were treated as independent dynamical realizations, producing 24 observations per activity group. Two-sided Welch’s t -tests were performed using the scipy.stats.ttest_ind function of the Python package scipy with equal_var = False . The corresponding p -values are denoted p comp and p int , respectively.

The stabilized configurational space was defined as the configurations in the ternary complex simulations that are also seen in the simulations of the monomers and binary complexes, respectively. The high rigidity of FKBP12 in both binary and ternary complexes allows us to approximate the stabilized configurational space using a frame-to-frame alignment scheme as a geometric filter.

Molecular glues (MGs) have emerged as a powerful modality in drug discovery, offering the unique ability to induce novel protein–protein interactions (PPIs) and target flat protein surfaces that have been previously considered inaccessible. − By stabilizing the interface between an E3 ligase (or another presenter protein) and a target protein, molecular glues can trigger downstream effects such as ubiquitination and degradation. , Compared to bifunctional PPI inducers such as proteolysis targeting chimeras (PROTACs), MGs often display higher cooperativity and are less susceptible to the hook effect (or prozone effect). − Cooperativity in induced-proximity systems has been described within the thermodynamic framework of three-body binding equilibria, while structural studies of PROTAC ternary complexes have demonstrated how favorable protein–protein interactions can drive cooperative ternary-complex formation. However, despite their potential, rational design and even optimization of molecular glues remain a significant challenge. While numerous computational approaches, including physics-based and machine learning methods, have been developed in recent years to facilitate ternary-complex prediction, these tools are still far from fully capturing the dynamics and determinants of cooperativity that govern ternary-complex formation (see the review in ref and references therein). Consequently, discovery often continues to rely on serendipity or extensive empirical screening. −

An example of this challenge is the system involving FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12) and MAPRE1 (microtubule associated protein RP/EB family member 1). In the recent work by Salcius et al., a macrocyclic MG R,S-SLF-1a ( 1a ) was discovered to induce interactions between FKBP12 and MAPRE1 ( Figure A). In the same work, the structure–activity relationship of the MAPRE1-recognition motif was studied by mutating two sites: the 4-piperidine moiety ( Figure A–B, circled in yellow) and the α-position ( Figure A–B, circled in red). Several modifications at the α-position of this site retain glue activity, but with a wide range of absolute cooperativity as determined by follow-up work ( Figure C and Table ). In contrast, modifications to the 4-piperidine moiety consistently impede MAPRE1 recruitment ( Figure D). The static picture from the crystal structure could not explain how these subtle changes influence cooperativity and glue activity.

In this work, we bridge the gap between the static structural data and observed cooperativity by investigating the dynamics of binary and ternary complexes using enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By extensively sampling the ensembles of the FKBP12-ligand complexes with and without MAPRE1 using replica exchange with solute scaling (REST2), we formulated the hypothesis that high cooperativity arises from the PPI in the specific “stabilized configurational space” that is shared in both ensembles. Based on the recently developed thermodynamic foundations of cooperativity, we established a computational pipeline to predict the cooperativity of new MG candidates. First, we proposed a model that correlates the experimental cooperativity and the computed PPI matrices by developing and evaluating the model using the previously reported variants of 1a . Subsequently, we applied the model to prospectively design novel variants of 1a and predict their cooperativity in silico . Five candidates were synthesized and experimentally tested (together with resynthesis and retesting of five previous compounds). Three of the novel compounds exhibit an apparent cooperativity similar to or higher than the previously known most cooperative retested compound 11 . Another one shows an apparent cooperativity similar to the second-most cooperative retested compound 6 . Our results demonstrate that incorporation of conformational dynamics and induced PPI analysis is a viable strategy for the rational design and optimization of cooperative MGs.

To investigate the difference between the inactive compounds and the active ones, four active compounds covering a wide range of apparent cooperativity ( 1a , 8 , 10 , and 11 , see Figure C) and four inactive compounds ( 1d , 2a , 2c , and 2d , see Figure D) were studied in the ternary complex (FKBP12-ligand-MAPRE1 = FLM) with MD simulations for 1 μs (three replicates). In addition, a ligand-free (apo) system was also simulated for comparison. During the simulations, a dynamic interface between the two proteins was observed, which sees the fluctuating formation and disappearance of “native” and “nonnative” contacts between FKBP12 and MAPRE1, differing mainly by the tilt motion of MAPRE1 ( Figure A–B). “Native” contacts are PPIs observed in the available crystal structure of the ternary complex, whereas PPIs only seen in the simulations are considered “nonnative”. While the apo system quickly lost most of the native contacts (as expected due to the very low affinity of FKBP12 to MAPRE1 in the absence of glues), no significant differences in terms of PPI contacts were observed between inactive and active compounds within the simulation time scale ( Figure C–D).

Next, we analyzed the pairwise interaction energies in the FLM ensembles with MM/GBSA. , Note that the interaction energies measured here only account for the interactions in the ternary ⟨⟩ FLM state and do not take into account the entropic effects before the ternary complexation. All eight compounds exhibit similar interaction energies with FKBP12, ⟨ Δ E F − L i n t ⟩ F L M ( Figure E), which agrees with the experimental findings that the modifications of 1a in the 4-piperidine moiety do not alter its affinity for FKBP12. , Similarly, the interaction energy between the protein partners, ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M , is largely unaffected by the type of ligand binding ( Figure F). On the other hand, the MAPRE1-ligand interaction energy, ⟨ Δ E M − L i n t ⟩ F L M , shows statistical significance between active and inactive compounds ( p = 1.881 × 10 –3 at the compound level and p = 2.126 × 10 –5 at the interface level, Figure G). This suggests that inactive compounds cannot induce the ternary complex due to the dual-binding criterion (i.e., a molecular stabilizer needs to possess some affinity for both proteins). Interestingly, while in most simulations of the active compounds more than 40% of the contacts between the two proteins were native (i.e., native contact ratio >0.4), the inactive compounds show an anticorrelation between the MAPRE1-ligand interaction strength and the native contact ratio (Spearman’s correlation coefficient ρ = −0.81 for inactive compounds, Figure H), which is consistent with the hypothesis that firm interaction between the ligand and MAPRE1 stabilizes ternary complex configurations that contain many native contacts. Further analysis of the time series of these features and the RMSD of each component is shown in Section S2 in the Supporting Information .

In contrast to other macrocyclic MGs such as cyclosporine A, FK506, and rapamycin, compound 1a in the FKBP12-MAPRE1 system shows a significant conformational discrepancy between the crystal structures of the binary and ternary complexes ( Figure A–B). Superposition of the crystal structures of FL (PDB ID: 9DCW) and FLM (PDB ID: 9CO5) shows that FKBP12 and the FKBP12-binding motif of 1a ( Figure A) remain rigid upon recruitment of MAPRE1 (TM score: 0.98). However, the MAPRE1-recognition motif of 1a adopts an alternative conformation in the ternary complex to avoid a steric clash with MAPRE1 ( Figure A). To characterize the conformational change of the MAPRE1-recognition motif between the binary and ternary complexes, we define the intermotif angle θ lig by computing the angle formed by the planes fitted on the two motifs ( Figure B). This angle θ lig corresponds to −35.06° in the FL structure and 32.63° in the FLM structure. The difference in the ligand configuration implies the necessity of a conformational selection and/or induced-fit mechanism during the FL to FLM formation process, which is not immediately clear from the static structures. A detailed description of the protocol to calculate θ lig is provided in Section S3 in the Supporting Information .

When monitoring θ lig in the conventional MD simulations of the binary (FL) and ternary (FLM) complexes, we noted differences between the three replicates, which suggested convergence issues ( Section S4 of the Supporting Information ). Thus, we performed enhanced-sampling MD simulations using REST2; only the REST2 results are shown in the following. In the FL and FLM simulations, θ lig peaked around the values observed in the crystal conformations ( Figure C–D). Notably, the simulations occasionally sampled a conformation with θ lig around zero in both FL and FLM ensembles ( Figure C–D), which we termed the intermediate ligand conformation. In the FLM complexes, this intermediate conformation coincides with the bending motion of MAPRE1, characterized by a large angle θ PPI between three helical domains shown in Figure C. As a similar intermediate ligand conformation is occasionally sampled in the FL ensemble, we hypothesize that these low-probability intermediate conformations in both ensembles could explain a MAPRE1 recruitment pathway, as discussed in the next section.

To determine whether the intermediate conformations can also be adopted by other active compounds, we studied seven active compounds reported in ref : 3 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , and 11 . In addition to the FL and FLM complexes, REST2 simulations were performed for the ligands alone in the aqueous solution. Figure E shows that all compounds can adopt a range of conformations with θ lig between ±80 ◦ when free in solution. When bound to FKBP12 (FL ensemble), only conformations with θ lig values between negative and around zero are accessible, which indicates that the binding pocket restricts the flexibility of the macrocycles. Intriguingly, conformations with negative θ lig values are no longer reachable when MAPRE1 binds to the FL binary complex to form the ternary complex. Instead, zero to positive θ lig are found for the ligands in the FLM ensemble. The fact that binding of MAPRE1 induces a stable ligand conformation that is rarely observed in the FL ensemble highlights the cooperative interplay between the ligand conformation, the ligand-MAPRE1 interaction, and native PPI contacts, which we shall discuss in the next section.

The observation of a distinct yet overlapping conformational space in Figure E suggests that the formation of the ternary complex may be facilitated by both conformational selection and the induced-fit mechanism. This means that there is a subregion of the configurational space (ensemble) of the binary FKBP12-ligand complex that is suited for recruitment of MAPRE1. Similarly, there is a subregion of the configurational space of the ternary complex where the conformations of FKBP12 and the ligand overlap with conformations observed in the binary complex. In the following, we call these subregions of the binary and ternary ensembles the stabilized configurational spaces , which we denote with the superscript s . The superscript * is used to denote the minimal-energy configuration revealed by crystallography. Based on our observations from the MD simulations, we can formulate a hypothesis for the binding pathway, which is depicted in Figure A.

First, the ligand in the FL complex could transition from the low-energy configuration (i.e., θ lig ≤ −10°, FL *) to the stabilized configuration FL s (where −10° ≤ θ lig ≤ 10°). Second, MAPRE1 is recruited by weak ligand-MAPRE1 interactions and nonnative PPI contacts (this step can be viewed as conformational selection). Once the FLM complex is formed in the stabilized configurational space (FLM s , where −10° ≤ θ lig ≤ 10°), the ligand undergoes another conformational change in the third step to strongly bind MAPRE1 and to induce native PPI contacts (FLM*, where θ lig ≥ 10°). The common ligand conformation shared in the FL s and FLM s ensembles is highlighted in the inset box of Figure A. Note that the putative pathway presented here is derived from observations from the equilibrium simulations and does not exclude alternative pathways of ternary-complex formation.

According to the thermodynamics of cooperativity, the precise identification of such stabilized configurational space in the FLM ensemble provides us with an opportunity to compute (and subsequently predict, see below) the cooperativity of the system. If we do not consider this stabilized configurational space and naively compare the FKBP12-MAPRE1 interaction energy calculated over the full ensemble ( ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M ) with the experimentally observed cooperativity, the correlation is not very good (Spearman coefficient ρ = 0.45, Figure B). The correlation is significantly improved (ρ = 0.90, Figure C) when considering only frames of the stabilized configurational space to compute the interaction energy between the two proteins ( ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M s ) . To determine this stabilized configurational space in practice, we aligned the FKBP12 structures frame-to-frame to compute whether a configuration of FL observed in the ternary FLM ensemble has a nonzero probability to occur in the binary FL ensemble (see Figure S41 in Section S5 in the Supporting Information for a schematic depiction of the procedure). Section S5 also contains more details about the frame-to-frame alignment procedure. Note that as the model was developed using only eight previously reported compounds, the retrospective correlation should be interpreted as model development rather than independent validation. The prospective compounds were selected before experimental testing, and their experimental results were not used to refit the model.

Encouraged by the high correlation between the experimental cooperativity and ⟨ Δ E F − M i n t ⟩ F L M s , our objective was to look for derivatives of 1a that show similar or higher cooperativity. We noticed that the two most cooperative compounds 10 and 11 ( Table ) have two geminal substituents at the α-position in the MAPRE1-recognition motif (red circle in Figure A). Furthermore, the substituent(s) at the α-position of four of the five most cooperative compounds ( 11 , 10 , 3 , and 1a ) are lipophilic. Based on these considerations, we screened commercial catalogues for amino-acid building blocks with two geminal substituents where the D -substituent is a methyl group (or part of a ring) and the L -substituent is lipophilic. As compound 6 , which showed the third highest cooperativity of the full set has a hydroxymethyl substituent at the α-position, we also considered some polar L -substituents. This produced 17 candidates, from which 12 were retained for prospective simulations based on their size and compatibility with the molecular-glue scaffold ( p0-pB , Figure A). We used the same procedure as described in the previous section and the model fitted from the parent compounds to estimate their cooperativity ( Figure B). From this, compounds p0 , p2 , p3 , p4 , and p6 were predicted as the most cooperative compounds and were submitted for synthesis and experimental validation. As a control, the lead compound ( 1a ), a moderately cooperative compound ( 6 ), a weakly cooperative compound ( 9 ), the most cooperative compound ( 11 ), and an inactive compound ( 1d ) from the literature were also resynthesized and tested in the same assays.

Absolute cooperativity α can be determined experimentally by either measuring K F‑L and K F‑LM or by measuring K M‑L and K FL‑M ( Figure A). However, due to the limits of the experimental assay, no exact binary binding affinity between the ligands and MAPRE1, K M‑L , could be determined ( E C 50 b i n a r y M A P R E 1 > 500 μ M ) and thus no absolute cooperativity could be obtained. The MAPRE1-binding titration experiment is discussed in Section S6.2 in the Supporting Information . The ranking of the α a p p F K B P 12 values of the known compounds agrees overall well with the absolute cooperativity α abs reported in ref ( Figure C). In line with previous findings that compound 1d , an epimer of 1a , binds strongly to FKBP12 but cannot recruit MAPRE1, we find weak or no cooperativity ( α a p p F K B P 12 < 1 ) for 1d in the new experiments. The active compounds 11 , 9 , and 6 exhibit apparent cooperativity ranging from 8 to 41. From the five prospective compounds, only p3 shows little cooperativity ( α a p p F K B P 12 = 2.2 ± 0.4 , Figure D). Three compounds yielded apparent cooperativity similar to or greater than that of the best parent compound 11 ( α app FKBP 12 = 41 ± 13 ) : p0 (38 ± 11), p2 (39 ± 9), and p6 (81 ± 44). Compound p4 (21 ± 7) showed apparent cooperativity similar to that of the second-best retested parent compound 6 (24 ± 7).

Since the dissociation constant between the two proteins K F − M D is independent of the compound, the relative value of the protein cooperativity is equivalent to the ratio of ternary dissociation constants γ 1 / γ 2 = K F L 2 − M D / K F L 1 − M D . The MAPRE1-reporter EC50 ratio is used as an assay-derived relative apparent-cooperativity metric under the same assay conditions and is not interpreted as absolute thermodynamic cooperativity. In Figure E, we show a good correlation (Pearson coefficient r = 0.77) between the apparent cooperativities α a p p F K B P 12 and γ a p p M A P R E 1 relative to the lead compound 1a measured by different labeled proteins, providing a strong cross-assay concordance.

In summary, we achieved our goal to rationally design novel variants with higher cooperativity based on the observations from the MD simulations. These positive results highlight the power of considering a dynamic picture in the design of molecular glues.

The rational design and optimization of molecular glues has long been hindered by the complexity of predicting the protein–protein interface dynamics. In this study, we demonstrated that the cooperativity of macrocyclic molecular glues for the FKBP12-MAPRE1 system cannot be adequately explained by static crystal structures alone. By employing MD simulations, we could formulate a putative pathway for the formation of the ternary complex and successfully designed variants of the lead compound 1a with similar or higher cooperativity.

Our MD simulations suggest that the modifications of the 4-piperidine moiety fail to form the ternary complex because of the less favorable MM/GBSA interaction energies, which is consistent with weaker MAPRE1 engagement. Using enhanced sampling, we further revealed an intermediate conformation of the ligand, which is sampled in both the binary FKBP12-ligand and the ternary FKBP12-ligand-MAPRE1 ensembles. The observed ensemble overlap is consistent with a putative pathway involving conformational selection followed by structural relaxation, although the equilibrium simulations do not establish the kinetic sequence. By only considering the configurations in the intermediate state, which we call the stabilized configurational space, a high correlation (Spearman coefficient ρ = 0.90) was found between the computed interaction energy between the two proteins in the ternary complex and the experimentally measured absolute cooperativity. Using this model, we estimated the cooperativity of a library of 12 prospective variants of lead 1a and selected five for synthesis and experimental testing. Of these five novel compounds, four showed higher apparent cooperativity than the parent lead compound 1a , and three of them showed similar or greater apparent cooperativity than the previously most cooperative compound 11 .

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to elaborate on the conformational changes of molecular glues upon the third-body binding event and to prospectively design highly cooperative glues by establishing and targeting the stabilized configurational space shared between binary and ternary ensembles using MD simulations. We anticipate that this work will encourage researchers in the field to include considerations of protein and ligand dynamics in the design of cooperative molecular glues.

The initial conformations of the active molecular glue compounds were generated using the ConstrainedEmbed function of RDKit version 2023.03 using as a template the conformation of 1a in the crystal structure of the binary complex with FKBP12 (PDB ID: 9DCW) and of the ternary complex (PDB ID: 9CO5) respectively. The generated conformers were exported as an SDF file and converted to mol2 files and energy-minimized with the MMFF94 force field using OpenBabel 3.1.0. Because of the change in stereochemistry, inactive compounds 1d , 2a , 2c , and 2d were generated by the Builder in PyMOL v2.5.5 and saved as a mol2 file for later parametrization.

The initial coordinates of the complexes are taken from the crystal structures with ligand 1a (PDB IDs: 9DCW and 9CO5) either retained ( 1a ), removed (apo system), or replaced (other compounds). The AMBER ff19SB force field was used for proteins, GAFF2 , for the ligands, OPC for water molecules, and Joung/Cheatham ion parameters for Na + and Cl – ions. Partial charges of the ligands were assigned with the AM1-BCC method implemented in the program antechamber .

The constructed complexes were solvated in a water box with a length of 1.2 nm from the complex edge in each dimension with 0.15 M NaCl using the program tleap from AmberTools22. All simulations were performed with AMBER 22.

Energy minimization was performed for a maximum of 5,000 cycles, comprising 2,500 steps of steepest descent followed by up to 2,500 steps of conjugate-gradient minimization. A positional restraint with a force constant of 418.4 kJ mol –1 nm –2 was applied to proteins and ligand atoms during minimization. Equilibration comprised two consecutive 125 ps NVT stages followed by two consecutive 125 ps NPT stages. A time step of 1 fs was used during equilibration. Positional-restraint force constants of 418.4, 209.2, 209.2, and 41.84 kJ mol –1 nm –2 were applied to protein and ligand atoms during the four successive equilibration stages. Following equilibration, three production replicas were initiated from the final restart file of the second NPT stage. Although the replicas shared the same initial coordinates and velocities, they were propagated using independently initialized Langevin random streams generated with the AMBER 22 default setting ig = −1 .

Simulations were carried out with a Langevin thermostat to keep the temperature at 295.15 K with a collision frequency of 1.0 ps –1 and a Monte Carlo barostat to keep the pressure at 1 bar. A nonbonded cutoff distance of 1 nm was used with PME , to treat the long-range electrostatic interaction. The simulations were integrated with a time step of 2 fs, using the SHAKE algorithm to constrain the bond lengths of bonds involving hydrogen with a relative geometrical tolerance of 10 –6 . The translational and rotational center-of-mass motion was removed every 1000 steps. Trajectories were printed every 500 ps in the production simulation for analysis.

For the enhanced-sampling simulations, the REST2 implementation in Amber22 called Replica Exchange with Arbitrary Degree of Freedom (REAF) was used by setting the flag gti_add_re = 6 . The scaling was only applied on the ligand degrees of freedom. A scaling factor (1-τ) between 1 and 0.4 was used with an even spacing in the linear scale between 12 replicas, i.e., τ k = {0.000, 0.05454, 0.10908, 0.16362, 0.21816, 0.27270, 0.32724, 0.38178, 0.43632, 0.49086, 0.54540, 0.59994}, where k indicates the replica index, was used for the binary and ternary complex simulations, and a linear scale between 14 replicas ranging between 1 and 0.25, i.e., τ k = {0.000, 0.05769, 0.11538, 0.17307, 0.23076, 0.28845, 0.34614, 0.40383, 0.46152, 0.51921, 0.57690, 0.63459, 0.69228, 0.74997}, was used for the ligand-only simulations. The enhanced-sampling simulations were initiated from the last frame of the second NPT equilibration and propagated for 200 ns with replica exchange attempted at every 100 steps. The exchange acceptance ratios were around 35% in the ligand-only and binary complexes, and around 20% in the ternary complexes between all neighboring replicas. The per-replica-pair exchange ratio is shown in Figure S37 in the Supporting Information . Trajectories of the REST2 simulations were printed every 20 ps. The analyses on the REST2 simulations were performed on the physical replica (τ 0 = 0).

From the crystal structure of the ternary complex with compound 1a , the “native” contacts between the two proteins were defined as the number of atoms from one protein within 5 Å of any heavy atom of the second protein using the nativecontact command from cpptraj in AmberTools22, which provides both native and nonnative contact counts. The same procedure was applied to the frames of the MD simulations. If an identified contact is not part of the “native” set obtained from the crystal structure, it was counted as “nonnative”. The native contact ratio was calculated as N nat /( N nat + N non‑nat ), where N nat and N non‑nat are the number of native and nonnative contact atoms. It indicates whether the interactions between the two proteins are similar to the ones observed in the ternary crystal structure.

As a simplified descriptor of the bending motion of the MAPRE1-binding core of the ligand observed between the binary and ternary crystal structures, the angle between the MAPRE1-binding core and the FKBP12-binding core ( Figure A) was calculated by measuring the angle between the two fitting planes, termed the intercore angle θ lig . A detailed description and illustration of the plane-fitting procedure is provided in Section S3 in the Supporting Information .

Active and inactive compounds were compared at both the compound and interface levels. For the primary compound-level analysis, the six interface values obtained from three simulations with two interfaces each were averaged for each compound, producing four compound-level observations per activity group. For the exploratory interface-level analysis, the six interface values from each compound were treated as independent dynamical realizations, producing 24 observations per activity group. Two-sided Welch’s t -tests were performed using the scipy.stats.ttest_ind function of the Python package scipy with equal_var = False . The corresponding p -values are denoted p comp and p int , respectively.

MAPRE1 (FVD1, PC24359–1) was labeled using an NHS-NT650 fluorophore according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 20 μM MAPRE1 was incubated with 60 μM NHS-NT650 dye in NHS labeling buffer supplemented with 0.01% Pluronic for 30 min at room temperature. Following labeling, samples were centrifuged for 10 min at 1500 g to remove aggregates. The degree of labeling was determined to be approximately 86%.

FKBP12 (CKU8, PD24502–1) was labeled using RED-tris-NTA second generation dye, exploiting the affinity of the tris-NTA moiety for the His-tag. For labeling, FKBP12 was incubated with RED-tris-NTA dye for 20 min at room temperature, followed by centrifugation for 10 min at 15000 g prior to use.

All compounds were prepared as stock solutions in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). For MAPRE1-binding experiments, a 1:2 serial dilution series consisting of 12 concentrations was prepared, starting from a highest compound concentration of 400 μM. For FKBP12 binding experiments, a 1:3 serial dilution series of 12 concentrations was prepared, starting from a highest compound concentration of 50 μM. Final DMSO concentrations were maintained at 2% (v/v) in all assay conditions.

All measurements were performed in assay buffer consisting of 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.01% Pluronic (nonionic triblock copolymers). Compound dilutions were mixed with concentrated labeled protein solutions to yield the final assay concentrations. Each condition was prepared in duplicate technical replicates within the same experiment. For FKBP12-binding assays, 80 nM FKBP12 was incubated with 10 nM RED-tris-NTA dye and subsequently assayed at a final concentration of 40 nM FKBP12 in the presence of 5 nM NTA fluorophore. For MAPRE1-binding assays, the labeled protein concentration was 5 nM.

After equilibration at room temperature, samples were measured at LED powers of 39.9%–100% depending on protein concentration (39.9% for 5 nM MAPRE1, 80.9% for 40 nM FKBP12). Fluorescence emission ratios at 670 and 650 nm were recorded. The ratio (670 nm/650 nm) was plotted as a function of compound concentration to determine EC50.

Labeled FKBP12 (CKU8, PD24502–1) was used as the fluorescent reporter protein at a final concentration of 40.0 nM. MAPRE1 (FVD1, PC24359–1) was added as an unlabeled binding partner at a fixed concentration of 10 μM.

The assay buffer consisted of 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, and 0.01% Pluronic F-127. Final DMSO concentrations were maintained at 2% (v/v) across all conditions. All compounds were prepared as DMSO stock solutions and assayed as 1:3 serial dilution series consisting of 12 concentrations, starting from a highest compound concentration of 20.0 μM and decreasing to 112.9 pM. Compound dilutions were mixed with concentrated labeled FKBP12 and MAPRE1 solutions to achieve the final assay concentrations. Each condition was measured once in duplicate technical replicates within the same experiment.

All measurements were performed on a Dianthus NT.23 PicoDuo instrument using an LED power of 77.6% (pico detector setting). Fluorescence emission ratios at 670 and 650 nm were recorded. The spectral shift ratio (670 nm/650 nm) was plotted as a function of compound concentration to assess ternary complex formation and to determine apparent binding affinities.

Ternary complex formation was assessed in the presence of unlabeled FKBP12 (CKU9, PD24504–1), which was included directly in the assay buffer at a fixed final concentration of 10 μM. Compound dilutions were mixed with labeled MAPRE1 and FKBP12-containing assay buffer to reach the indicated final concentrations. Each condition was measured once in duplicate technical replicates within the same experiment.
